sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Anima** ​(*anima*) — ‌Soul, Breath, ‌Life Force ​· Breath, ​air, soul ​— belongs ​to the ​Greek tradition, ‌where it ​is catalogued ​under ‌the domain ​"Soul, Breath, ‌Life Force". ​The name ‌means "Breath, ​air, soul"[^1].

​**Anima** is ​the Latin ​word for ​breath, air, ‌and ​— by ‌extension — ​the soul ‌or life-force ​that animates ‌a living ​body. It ‌names one ​of the ​most ancient ‌equations ‌in Western ‌thought: that ​the difference ​between a ‌corpse and ​a living ​person is ‌the presence ​of breath. ​From this ‌simple ​observation Latin ‌developed a ​rich vocabulary ​of animation, ​soul, and ​spirit that ‌still shapes ‌modern psychology, ​religion, and ‌biology.[^2]

PuniCodex ​restores ​the name ‌as **Anima** ‌and serves ‌its temple ‌at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/anima/). The ‌original preserves ​one prosodic ​feature — ​stress or ‌vowel ​length — ​rather than ​both, which ‌places the ​name in ​Tier 2. ​The plain ‌ASCII form ​*anima* survives ‌as a ​modern ‌convenience imposed ​by the ‌early domain-name ‌system; the ​restoration, not ​the fallback, ​is the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
No ​indigenous written ‌attestation ‌survives for ​this ​name; ​**Anima** is ​a ​scholarly transliteration ‌of ​the reconstructed ​spoken ‌form. Etymologically ​the ‌name ​means "Breath, ‌air, ​soul"[^1].

The ​ASCII ​form *anima* ​survives ​only because ‌the ​early ‌domain-name system ​could ‌not carry ​diacritics; ‌it is ​a ‌technological compromise, ​not ​an ‌ancient spelling. ‌The ‌Unicode restoration ​**Anima** ​recovers the ‌full ​diacritic detail ​of ‌the ​scholarly transliteration ​directly ‌in the ​address ‌bar. The ​original ​preserves ​one prosodic ​feature ‌— stress ‌or ​vowel length ‌— ​rather than ​both, ‌which ‌places the ‌name ‌in Tier ​2.

‌The letter-by-letter ​transformation ​runs:

- ​**a** ‌→ ​**A** — ​A ​uppercase
- ‌**n** ​→ **n** ​— ​n same
‌- ​**i** ‌→ **i** ​— ‌i same
​- ‌**m** → ‌**m** ​— m ​same
​- ​**a** → ‌**a** ‌— a ​same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of the ‌name is ​**/ˈa.nɪ.ma/** — ​Classical Latin ​Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**a-** — ​Short open ​vowel [a], ‌the first ​syllable of ‌the Latin ​word ‌for breath ​and soul.
​- **-ni-** ​— Short ​[nɪ], with ​the vowel ‌reduced ​and unstressed ‌in Classical ​Latin.
- ‌**-ma** — ​Short [ma], ‌the feminine ​noun ‌ending that ​gives the ​word its ‌grammatical form.

‌For the ‌modern speaker, ​the closest ​approximation ‌is: 'AH-nih-mah' ​— stress ​the first ‌syllable; the ​middle vowel ​is short ‌and ​light.

Kindred ‌and historical ​forms of ​the name:

​- **Latin** ​— anima, ‌breath, ‌air, life-force, ​soul
- ‌**Greek equivalent** ​— ψυχή ​(psychē), the ‌breath-soul; πνεῦμα ‌(pneuma), breath-spirit

‌Anima ‌is a ​Latin word, ‌not a ​Greek proper ​name. It ​has no ‌indigenous ​alphabetic 'original ​script' other ​than the ‌Latin alphabet. ​The ASCII ​form anima ​is ‌already the ​Latin spelling; ‌the restoration ​capitalises the ‌proper-noun form ​as a ‌scholarly citation. ‌Because ​no distinctive ​diacritic or ​special letter ​is added, ‌the entry ‌is Tier ​2.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The ​original ‌script for ‌this ​greek ​name ​has not ​yet ​been ‌added ​to PUNICODEX. ​The ‌form ​shown ‌is a ​scholarly ‌transliteration.[^1]

​The ​form **Anima** ​is ​therefore ​a ‌scholarly transliteration ​rather ‌than ​an ‌attested ancient ​spelling; ‌it ​encodes ‌the reconstructed ​sound ​of ‌the ‌name for ‌modern ​use, ​and ‌no mark ​in ​it ‌is ​decorative.

Anima ​is ‌a ​Latin ‌word. It ​has ​no ​'original ​script' in ‌the ‌sense ​of ‌Greek or ​cuneiform; ​its ‌canonical ‌form is ‌the ‌Latin ​spelling ‌**anima**. The ​ASCII ​form ​*anima* ‌already represents ​the ​Latin ​spelling ‌exactly. The ​restoration ​**Anima** ​is ‌therefore the ​capitalised ‌proper-noun ​citation ‌form, not ​a ‌phonetic ‌recovery. ​The appropriate ​label ​is ​'Scholarly ‌Transliteration' or ‌simply ​'Latin'.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Anima** ​is the ‌Latin ‌word for ​breath, air, ​and ​— by ​extension ​— the ‌soul or ​life-force ​that animates ‌a ​living body. ‌It ​names one ‌of the ​most ​ancient equations ​in ​Western thought: ​that ‌the difference ​between a ‌corpse ​and a ‌living ​person is ‌the presence ​of ‌breath. From ​this ​simple observation ‌Latin ‌developed a ‌rich vocabulary ​of ​animation, soul, ‌and ​spirit that ​still ‌shapes modern ​psychology, religion, ​and ‌biology.[^1]

### ​Breath

‌The literal ​meaning of ​anima: ​the air ​drawn ‌in and ‌expelled ​by living ‌creatures.

### ​Soul

​In philosophy ‌and ‌theology anima ‌becomes ‌the immaterial ​principle that ‌gives ​life and, ​later, ​the rational ‌soul.

### ​Life ​Force

The ​active ‌power that ​distinguishes ​the living ​from the ‌dead, ​the moving ‌from ​the still.

‌### ​Inspiration

Literally ‌'breathing in' ‌— ​the moment ​when ​life, ideas, ​or the ‌divine ‌enter the ​self.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Anima is ​not a mythological ‌character in the ‌Greek or Roman ​sense; it is ​a concept that acquired ​a long philosophical ​and theological history. ​Its 'mythology' is ‌therefore the story ​of how breath ​became soul, and ‌how soul became ​one of the ‌foundation stones of ​Western psychology.[^1]

### The ‌Breath of Life ​(Roman thought)

In ​Classical Latin anima ​first means breath, ​air, or breeze. ​Cicero uses it ‌for the vital ​breath that sustains ‌life, and Lucretius describes ​the soul as ‌a subtle, airy ​stuff mixed with ‌blood and heat, ​dispersed at death. ‌The word thus ​begins as a ​physical fact and ‌only gradually becomes ‌a metaphysical principle.[^2]

### ‌The Rational Soul ​(Christian theology)

Early ​Latin Christianity adopted ‌anima as the ​standard translation for ​Greek psychē and ‌Hebrew nephesh. Augustine's ​*De anima* and ​later scholastic treatises ‌made the anima rationalis ​the immortal, thinking ‌part of the ​human person, created ​by God and ​destined for salvation ​or damnation.

### ‌Jung's Anima (Modern ‌psychology)

In C. ​G. Jung's analytical ‌psychology the anima is ​the unconscious feminine ​image in the ‌male psyche, the ‌soul-figure that mediates ‌between the ego ‌and the unconscious. ​The term preserves ‌the Latin sense ​of soul while ​giving it a new, ​psychological meaning: the ‌anima is not ​a metaphysical substance ​but an inner ​figure shaped by ‌culture and personal ​history.

### Animation ​and Life (Modern ​language)

English words such ‌as animal, animate, ​animation, and equanimity ‌all descend from ​anima. Each preserves ‌a different shade ​of the original ‌meaning: the living, ‌the moving, the ​inspired, and the ​balanced soul. The word ​has travelled from ​biology to cinema ‌without ever fully ‌losing its connection ​to breath.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
The ​Latin ‌anima ‌overlaps ​with ​Greek ​psychē, Hebrew ​nephesh, ​Sanskrit ‌ātman, ​and ​Greek ‌pneuma. ​All ‌of ​these ‌terms ​begin ​with ​breath or ​wind ​and ‌develop ​into ‌concepts ​of ‌soul, ​spirit, ‌or ​self. ‌In ​medieval philosophy ​anima ‌became ‌the ‌bridge ​between ​Aristotelian ‌biology ​and ​Christian ‌theology, ​a ​development ‌that shaped ​European ‌thought ​until ​the ​early ​modern ‌period. ‌In ​modern ‌psychology ​it ​survives ‌as Jung's ‌anima ‌and ‌as ​the ‌root ​of ​'animation,' ​the ‌art ​of ​giving ​apparent life ‌to ​images.[^1]

​Within ​the ‌Greek ​tradition, ‌closely ​related ‌names ​in ‌the ‌corpus ​include [[acheron|Achérōn]], ​[[achilleus|Achilleús]], ​[[adamas|Adámas]], ​[[aer|Aḗr]], ‌[[aither|Aithḗr]], ‌and ​[[ajax|Aias]].

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or artifact ​in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is yet ​assigned ​to ‌Anima ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence should ​be ​read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Greek name ​of ‌this ​type ‌the ​material ‌record is ​expected ‌to ​be ​thin, ‌and ‌the ‌primary evidence ​remains ​the ‌textual ​testimony ​gathered ‌in the ​Scholarly ​Sources ‌section[^1].

​Were ‌such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ​would ‌take ‌recognizable ​forms: votive ‌or ​dedicatory ​inscriptions ‌naming ‌Anima, ‌sanctuary ‌or cult ​remains ‌tied ​to ​soul ​and ‌iconography matching ​its ​traditional ​attributes ‌(breath ​or ​wind and ​bird). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be ‌weighed ​against the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name ​before entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
To ​meditate ‌on Anima ‌is ​to ​meditate on ​the ​boundary ​between body ‌and ​whatever ​we call ‌the ​self. ‌Breath ​is the ‌one ​physiological ​process that ​can ​be ​voluntary or ‌automatic; ​it ‌links the ​conscious ‌will ​to ‌the autonomic ​body. ‌The ​Latin word ​reminds ‌us ‌that the ‌soul ​was ​not originally ‌imagined ​as ​a ‌ghost in ​a ​machine ‌but as ​the ‌very ​fact of ​being ​alive.

​In ‌a digital ‌age, ​when ‌consciousness is ​often ​modelled ‌as computation, ‌Anima ‌asks ‌a simpler ​question: ‌what ​is ​it that ​makes ‌a ​living thing ​living? ​The ‌answer may ​not ​be ​a substance ‌but ​a ‌process ​— the ‌continuous ​exchange ‌of inner ‌and ​outer, ​self and ​world, ​that ‌breath so ‌perfectly ​symbolizes.[^1]
